100f7ce28c.b: Observed on Amāvāsyā tithi of Āśvayujaḥ (lunar) month (Pradōṣaḥ/paraviddha).
100f7ce28c.d: Gives light even to Naraka-vasis; Also, Bali was sent to Paatalam on this day.

10125e4973.b: Observed on Śukla-Saptamī tithi of Vaiśākhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
10125e4973.d: Worship Surya Bhagavan in a vessel (kumbha) filled with sugar, followed by dānam of the same.
10125e4973.s:
𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀𑌂 𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌮𑌷𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌿𑌨𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌃॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑌿𑌲𑍈𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑍈𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌮𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌲𑍇𑌪𑌨𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌿𑌲𑍇 𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌮𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌖𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑍁𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌕𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍈 𑌨𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌧𑍂𑌪𑌂 𑌨𑌿𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌪𑌯𑍇𑌦𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌂 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌂𑌵𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌯 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌮𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌲𑍇𑌪𑌨𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌮𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍀𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑌠𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑌾𑌹𑌿 𑌸𑌨𑌾𑌤𑌨॥  
𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌗𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌪𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍌।  
𑌸𑍌𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌾॥  
𑌅𑌹𑍋𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌗𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌦𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌃।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍁𑌷𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌨𑌿𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌭𑍋𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌘𑍃𑌤𑌪𑌾𑌯𑌸𑍈𑌃।  
𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑍀𑌤𑌾𑌤𑍈𑌲𑌲𑌵𑌣𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌮𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌥 𑌵𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌚𑌰𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌃॥  
𑌶𑌯𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑍀𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌲𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣𑌾𑌥 𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌾॥  
𑌦𑌶𑌭𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌭𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌕𑍇𑌣𑍈𑌕𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃।  
𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌾𑌠𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌬𑌤𑍋 𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌬𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌵𑌃।  
𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌪𑍇𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑌦𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌗𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾 𑌚 𑌪𑌰𑌂 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍋𑌪𑌮𑌃।  
𑌇𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾 𑌰𑌵𑍇𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾 𑌹𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌃॥  
𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌷𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌜𑌿𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌮𑌨𑍀 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌦𑌾𑌯𑌿𑌨𑍀।  
𑌯𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌰𑌯𑌾 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌸 𑌵𑍈 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 ௧௧௬ 𑌅𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇---  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌷𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌮𑍇 𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍁॥௨௧॥  
𑌅𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌬𑌤𑍋 𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌬𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌵𑌃॥  
𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌪𑍇𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌿 𑌚𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌗𑌯𑌵𑍇𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌵𑌃॥௨௨॥  
𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾 𑌚 𑌤𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍋𑌪𑌮𑌾।  
𑌇𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾 𑌰𑌵𑍇𑌰𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾 𑌹𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌃॥௨௩॥  
𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌾𑌜𑌿𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑍋𑌪𑌶𑌮𑌨𑍀 𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌨𑍀॥௨௪॥  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌭𑍋𑌜𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍍॥௨௫॥  
𑌯𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌰𑌯𑌾 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌸 𑌵𑍈 𑌸𑌦𑍍𑌗𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍।

10364cc9fe.b: Total lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈12.0 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (mukha/ascending).
10364cc9fe.d: Umbral magnitude: 1.36 (parimāṇa ≈12.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 11:34►02:25 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra śatabhiṣak/pūrvaprōṣṭhapadā/uttaraprōṣṭhapadā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or punarvasuḥ (anujanma) or viśākhā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: kumbhaḥ, mīnaḥ, karkaṭaḥ, vr̥śchikaḥ get more ashubha phala, mithunam, siṁhaḥ, tulā, makaraḥ somewhat ashubha, mēṣaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ, kanyā, dhanuḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
10364cc9fe.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

104e6956dc.d: It is said in the Vishnu Purāṇam, that if the Amavasya of Magha month coincides with the nakashatra of Varuna, i.e. Shatabhishak, the pitr̥s are overjoyed, and do not obtain it unless they have accumulated a lot of punya! If it is Shravishtha, then the pitr̥s are satisfied for (ten) thousand years. amāvāsyā of māgha month.
104e6956dc.s:
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌮𑍍---  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌕𑌦𑌾𑌚𑌿𑌦𑍁𑌪𑍈𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌣𑍇𑌨।  
𑌋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌣 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌃 𑌸 𑌵𑌰𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌨𑍃𑌪 𑌲𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌸𑍌॥  
𑌗𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍇𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑌦𑌾 𑌨𑍁 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾 𑌮𑌘𑌾 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍂𑌯𑌃।  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌤𑍋𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌤𑌨𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍈𑌃॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇 𑌧𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌭𑍂𑌪𑌾𑌲 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌜𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌜𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌃॥

11addeac28.d: Preceptor Śrī Chandraśekhara adorned the Pīṭha for seventeen years. He reached his eternal beatitude on the eighth day of the black fortnight in the month of Māgha of the year Parābhava. The name of this preceptor before initiation was Svāminātha. Parents were well-known Maṅgalāmbikā and Sītārāmaśāstri. His place of siddhi was village Kalavai in Śalivahana era 1830. The adhishthanam is at the Kalavai Brindavanam, at https://maps.app.goo.gl/j4cKLo3CWWJeBFJC9.
11addeac28.s:
𑌸𑍀𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌚𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌨𑌯𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌥𑌾𑌭𑌿𑌧𑍋  
𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑍀 𑌸𑌂𑌯𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸 𑌜𑌾𑌤 𑌉𑌦𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑌟𑍁।  
𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌿𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌨𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌨𑍍  
𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌤𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌮𑌠𑍇 𑌸𑍁𑌵𑌿𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌣 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍂𑌰𑌿𑌣𑌾॥௧௯॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍇𑌖𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌶 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌭𑌵𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌧𑌾𑌮 𑌨𑌿𑌜𑌂 𑌯𑌯𑍌॥௨௦॥  
—𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌮𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌰𑍀 𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍

124a2e4ee1.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑌰𑍇।  
  
𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑍈 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍇𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌰𑍇।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑍋 𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌮𑍍॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇-𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍇  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇---  
𑌸𑌿𑌂𑌹𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍌 𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌾 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍇 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌃,  
𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌚𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯-𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌦𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌮𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂  
𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌊𑌰𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌨𑌿𑌷𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌃।  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇-𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍇  
𑌵𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---  
𑌨𑌭𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌃 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍋 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇𑌯𑌃---  
𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌿 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑌶 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚 𑌚।  
𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌨𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑍀𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌚𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌂 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌶𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌤𑍇॥  
  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌚॥௨௦॥  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌥 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇।  
𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௨௧॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌚 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌘𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌮𑍇।  
𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿॥௨௨॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰 𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌃।  
𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌣𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍॥௨௩॥  
𑌤 𑌏𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑌸𑌃 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾 𑌨𑍃𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍈𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌮𑍋𑌘𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌷𑌃॥௨௪॥  
𑌏𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑍍‍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌨𑍃𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௨௫॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 ௭-௧௪

12bcfa3019.d: While the Mahalaya Paksha (typically the 5th (Dark) Paksha from āṣāḍha) is the most important time to perform pitr̥-śrāddha, our Shaastras have specified the gauṇakāla or secondary timings for the performances for these very important śrāddhas. These śrāddhas can be performed in this paksha, in case circumstances prevented the performance of the śrāddhas in the uttama-kāla. Today marks the beginning of the 7th (Dark) Paksha from āṣāḍha.
12bcfa3019.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌗𑍌𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍋𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑍇---  
𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌯𑍋𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑌰𑌃।  
𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌤𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾॥  
𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌿 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑍋 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈 𑌸𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌶𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌤𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍀 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌕𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍋 𑌵𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌕𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌶𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾।  
𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌵𑌨𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍁𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌮𑍍॥  
---𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥-𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑌿𑌃

12cb83ef48.s:

𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌽𑌨𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌧𑍀𑌯𑍀𑌤 𑌕𑌦𑌾𑌚𑌨।  
𑌚𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌗𑍌𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿—  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍀 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍀𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿॥  
𑌉𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍀𑌰𑌾𑌰𑌭𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍍।

𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌰𑌥𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।

132a2b8687.b: Observed on Citrā nakshatra of Karkaṭaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
132a2b8687.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Perumizhalai Kurumba Nayanmar was a great devotee of both Bhagavan Shiva and his Guru, Sundaramurthi Nayanmar. He believed that the Guru is God in human form and devoted himself wholeheartedly to Sundarar. Through his faith and devotion, Kurumba Nayanmar attained all the Siddhis (psychic powers) and experienced deep ecstasy in both Shiva Bhakti and Guru Bhakti.

When Sundarar was about to leave the mortal world and attain his place in Shiva's abode, Kurumba Nayanmar was unable to bear the thought of being separated from his beloved Guru. Using his yogic powers, he learned of Sundarar's impending departure and decided to join him in the divine realm. Through the practice of Shiva Yoga, Kurumba Nayanmar shed his mortal body and reached Shiva's abode a day before Sundarar.
132a2b8687.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

13edf123d2.d: Sītāpati, son of Premeśa, on the banks of river Pinākinī, received at the age of seventeen years, initiation into asceticism from preceptor Śrī Chandracūḍa; that eminent preceptor defeated in debates great scholar poets Śrī Harsha, Abhinavagupta and others and wandered three times throughout the earth. This preceptor Cidvilāsa, revered by all, spread the tenets of Advaita through his eloquent teachings reached Cidambaram; worshipping the Muktiliṅga, He disappeared in the air in the very presence of the onlookers all around, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha in the year Siddharthi. This preceptor Śrī Advaitānandabodhendra, also known as the author of Brahmavidyābharaṇavivaraṇa and other works and a lion to the elephants, viz., refuting the views of Śrī Harsha, Abhinavagupta and others in debates. His preceptorship spread over thirty-four years.
13edf123d2.s:
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌮𑍇𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌕𑌿𑌨𑍀𑌤𑌟𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌃 𑌸𑍂𑌨𑍁𑌃 𑌸 𑌸𑍀𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌤𑌿𑌃

1444b78248.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in āśrēṣā karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°30′35.59″.
1444b78248.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°30′35.59″, 0°30′28.28″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at āśrēṣā-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°44′28.87″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -2.04, elongation 1°45′14.53″ W). śukraḥ at āśrēṣā-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°13′53.27″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 1°14′56.74″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
1444b78248.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।

1457ef9af9.s:

𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇---  
𑌅𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌭𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍇 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌭𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍈𑌃।

𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑍈 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌣𑌾𑌭𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌖𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌨𑍇𑌨 ‘𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌂 𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌤𑍋𑌯𑌮𑍍’ 𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣। 𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾---  
𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌯𑍋𑌨𑌿𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮।  
𑌉𑌦𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌲𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌽𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍋𑌽𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍍॥௧॥  
𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌂 𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌤𑍋𑌯𑌂 𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌚।  
𑌉𑌦𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌲𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌽𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍋𑌽𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍍॥௨॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌶𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌶 𑌵𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌤𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌵।  
𑌉𑌦𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌲𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌽𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍋𑌽𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍍॥௩॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍇𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍। 𑌰𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌥𑌮𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃, 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇-𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌥𑌮𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌭𑍇𑌦𑌃।

15557594e0.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃---  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌛𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚॥  
𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍀 𑌚 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾।  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍀 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌦𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌆𑌸𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---   
𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌲𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌹𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁।  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥

1586396341.b: Observed on Śukla-Tr̥tīyā tithi of Bhādrapadaḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti).
1586396341.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃---  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌛𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚॥  
𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍀 𑌚 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾।  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍀 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌦𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌆𑌸𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---   
𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌲𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌹𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁।  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥

158abcb9b0.b: Observed on Śukla-Ēkādaśī tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
158abcb9b0.d: Jyeshtha Devi (Kali wife), Varuni (Sesha wife), Sauparni (Garuda wife), Apsaras, Gandharvas, Airavata, Ucchaisrava, Dhanvantari, Parijatam, Kamadhenu born from Milk ocean

15c39d1960.b: Observed on Śukla-Aṣṭamī tithi of Jyaiṣṭhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).

15c42b48d1.d: Dvadashi tithi, combined with Shravana nakshatra is extremely special. In this case, it is acceptable to skip the Ekadashi fast and fast primarily on Shravana Dvadashi. Those who are able to fast on both days may fast on both days. The Shravana Dvadashi fast is nitya, meaning there is a pratyavāya for not performing it. It is said the the puṇya accumulated over the previous five years is destroyed, by not fasting on Shravana Dvadashi.
15c42b48d1.s:
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌦𑍀𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌮𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌕𑌲𑌶𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌯𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌨𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂  
𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋𑌪𑌵𑍀𑌤𑍋𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌹𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌉𑌪𑍋𑌷𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌦𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌨𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌂   
𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌜𑌲𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌘𑌟𑌂 𑌛𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃---  
𑌨𑌮𑍋 𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦 𑌬𑍁𑌧𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌕।  
𑌅𑌘𑍌𑌘𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍌𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵॥  
---𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌸𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍌  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌮𑌾 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃।  
𑌨 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌾 𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌵 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌶𑌬𑍍𑌦 𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌲𑌿𑌙𑍍𑌗𑍋𑌽𑌪𑍀𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌃। 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍇𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑌾𑌠𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌂 𑌚।  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍋 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪।  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌕𑌲𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌲𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤 𑌸 𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇𑌯𑍋 𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌕𑌃॥  
---𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍇 𑌸𑍈𑌵𑍋𑌪𑍋𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾।  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌚 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌚𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌶𑍃𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌲𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍃𑌦𑍍 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌃।  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌶𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌂 𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌤𑌿𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌂 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍋𑌹𑌤𑌿॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌶𑍇𑌦𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌸 𑌏𑌵 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑍋 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌶𑍃𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌲𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌿𑌤𑌃॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌚।  
𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀-𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾। 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌪𑌠𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌚 𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌶𑍇𑌦𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿। 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌮𑌤𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤-𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌶𑍃𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌲𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿।  
---𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍌  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌶𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌵𑌸𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌃---  
𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌾 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌤𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍇𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌣𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌉𑌪𑍋𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌹𑌾॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌜𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌮𑍍॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍂𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌮𑌪𑍋𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌵 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌧𑍋𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌭𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌃॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑍈𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿।  
𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌫𑌲𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌚 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌸𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌶𑍃𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌲𑌾 𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇𑌯𑌾 𑌸𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌫𑌲𑌦𑌾𑌯𑌿𑌨𑍀॥  
𑌗𑍌𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌚 𑌸𑍍𑌪𑍃𑌶𑍇𑌦𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌸 𑌏𑌵 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑍋 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌶𑍃𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌲𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌕𑌃॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌇𑌯𑌂 𑌚 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍋𑌪𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑍋 𑌨𑍋𑌪𑍋𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿 𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌤𑌿𑌃।  
𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥  
𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌤𑍍   
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌯𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇---  
𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌨𑌭𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌉𑌪𑍋𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌮𑌪𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌹𑍃𑌷𑍀𑌕𑍇𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍇।  
𑌉𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌣𑌨𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌰𑌃॥  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑍌𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌂 𑌚 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌮𑍍।

15c5ad59ea.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′41.60″.
15c5ad59ea.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′41.60″, 0°51′18.65″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′50.36″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°43′04.62″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′31.95″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′41.89″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

176a6787ff.b: Observed on Mūlā nakshatra of Vr̥ṣabhaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
176a6787ff.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar (Thirunavukkarasar), Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavachakar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

The 28th of the Nayanmars, Thirugnana Sambandar, born to a devout Brahmana couple---Shivapada Hridayar and Bhagavatiar---in 7th-century Sirkazhi, was an answer to his father's prayers for a son who would revive the glory of Shaivism. At the age of three, during a visit to the Sattainathar Shiva Temple, Sambandar was left by his parents near a pond. While alone, he began to cry and was comforted and fed by Devi Parvati and Bhagavan Shiva, appearing as Thoniappar. His parents found milk on his lips and upon questioning, Sambandar pointed skyward and spontaneously composed his first hymn, “Thodudaiya Seviyan”, symbolizing his reception of divine wisdom or Shivajnanam. This event marked him as Thirugnana Sambandar, the Nayanmar of divine knowledge, and Aludaiya Pillayar, Bhagavan’s child.

Celebrated as Tala Vendan, the unrivaled master of rhythm in the Periyapuranam, Sambandar demonstrated prodigious talents from a young age. By the time he was seven, he began singing about the Vedas and authored a significant collection of hymns, forming volumes 1-3 of the Thirumurai.

Sambandar, from an early age, showed remarkable spiritual gifts, composing and singing hymns in praise of Bhagavan Shiva, now known as Thevaram. During a pilgrimage, he met Tiru Neelakanta Yazhpanar (the 61st of the Nayanmars), an expert musician, who became his constant companion. Sambandar's journey was filled with miraculous events --- he was given a pair of golden cymbals by Bhagavan Shiva, received a pearl palanquin from Bhagavan to ease his travels, and his divine hymns healed the sick and performed wonders.

In Madurai, dominated by Jainism, Sambandar played a crucial role in re-establishing Shaivism. He miraculously cured the Jain king of a burning ailment using sacred ash and defeated the Jains in various spiritual challenges. His actions led to the king embracing Shaivism and the resurgence of the faith in the region.

Sambandar’s life was marked by his profound devotion and the numerous miracles he performed. He brought a merchant's dead daughter back to life and helped many others through his spiritual powers. As his wedding approached at the age of 16, Sambandar prayed to Shiva for liberation. During his wedding, a miraculous blaze of light, the Shiva Jyoti, appeared. As he recited the “Panchakshara Padigam”, everyone present --- including Tiruneelanakka Nayanmar, Muruga Nayanmar and Tiruneelakanta Yazhpanar --- were absorbed into a divine light, merging with Bhagavan Shiva! His legacy continues to influence and inspire Shaivite devotion and music.
176a6787ff.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

17a5245ea2.b: Observed on Śatabhiṣak nakshatra of Mīnaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
17a5245ea2.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme.

In the Chola kingdom's Tiruvarur, there lived a devout worshipper named Dandi Adigal. Born without sight, he continually chanted the Panchaksharam and envisioned Bhagavan inwardly. He regularly visited the temple for pradakshinam and prayers.

Adigal aspired to expand a temple-side tank, bordered by Jaina residences. Despite his blindness, he resolved to undertake this task, driven by unwavering faith. He ingeniously set up a system with ropes and posts, using them to navigate and execute the digging. His efforts caught the attention of the nearby Jainas, who, envious of his progress, attempted to dissuade him, citing the sin of harming insects during excavation. Undeterred, Adigal confidently asserted that no harm would come to any creature by divine grace. The Jainas, unimpressed, forcefully took his digging tools away.

Heartbroken, Adigal sought solace in the temple, where Bhagavan appeared in his dream, promising assistance. Simultaneously, Bhagavan also visited the king in a dream, urging him to address Adigal's troubles. Subsequently, at a royal assembly, Adigal proclaimed his faith in Bhagavan Shiva and declared that divine will could restore his sight while the Jainas might lose theirs. As he emerged from the tank, chanting the holy Panchaksharam, his sight was miraculously restored, and the Jainas were struck blind. Astonished by this divine intervention, the king expelled the Jainas and reinforced the people's faith in Bhagavan. Dandi Adigal ultimately achieved enlightenment.
17a5245ea2.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

17ca630566.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′54.31″.
17ca630566.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′54.31″, 0°33′44.00″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°40′20.96″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.13, elongation 10°14′15.55″ W). śaniḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°14′15.28″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.70, elongation 10°20′38.04″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

18e1af24a9.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Gananathar, a devout Brahmana from Sirkali, was the 38th of the Nayanmars. He was revered for his deep devotion to Bhagavan Shiva and was a source of spiritual guidance for many. Recognizing the varied abilities of those who sought his advice, he engaged them in service activities related to the temple, such as cleaning, making garlands, gardening, and lamp lighting. This approach not only transformed these individuals into Shiva Bhaktas but also infused a sense of devotion in them. Additionally, Gananathar was deeply devoted to Jnana Sambandar. All these great attributes contributed to him earning the grace of Bhagavan Shiva.
18e1af24a9.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

192e59ed48.d:
When the transit of the Sun (saṅkrānti) happens in the second half of the day (aparāhṇa) and before midnight, the second half of the day form a puṇyakāla for various observances. In addition to 16 ghatikas on either side of the transition, and specific puṇyakālas like ṣaḍaśīti, viṣṇupadī etc., this is also useful, especially in cases where the other puṇyakālas are inconvenient for appropriate performance of rituals such as snāna, dāna, tarpaṇa, etc.

While the nirayana puṇyakāla-s are well known, marked by the transit of the Sun into various rāśī-s (which confer the name to the corresponding saura month), there are also ayana-s and sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s, which mark the position of the Sun above the Northern or Southern parts of the Earth. These determine the r̥tu-s, and also the very famous uttarāyaṇa and dakṣināyana (movement of the Sun towards North or South, respectively). While these two types of puṇyakāla-s (sāyana and nirayana) coincided millennia ago, there has been a gradual precession of the equinoxes, owing to the nature of the Earth's rotation, causing the sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s to happen about 24 days before the nirayana saṅkramaṇa-s. In that era, uttarāyaṇa coincided with makara-saṅkramaṇa and dakṣināyana coincided with karkaṭaka-saṅkramaṇa, and the mēsa and tulā saṅkramaṇa-s corresponded to the equinoxes, when the Sun rises direct East (and sets direct West).

Many Dharma Shastra texts recognise the separate puṇyakāla-s for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. The vachanam of Jaabaali Maharshi is mentioned above, where he says that the puṇyakāla-s are identical (in their reckoning) for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. In the Pulastya Siddhanta, the anushthanas which are to be performed in this sayana punya kala just like nirayana are explicitly stated: snāna, dāna, japa, śrāddha, vrata, hōma, etc. In Kala Madhava, which is considered as the source text of the kala vicharas of the Dikshitiya, it is said in the 5th prakarana that,  meṣādi-saṅkrāntayo yasmin dine bhavanti tasmād dināt pūrvebhyaḥ ekādaśabhyo dinebhyaḥ prācīne dine, noting that Sayana Sankramanas occurred ~11 days before the day when the Mesha Sankramanas etc occur. Further references are seen in Dharma Sindhu first pariccheda, Jayasimha Kalpadruma sankranti nirnaya and Nirnaya Sindhu first pariccheda. There are also ample references in Vedas, illustrating how Ayana-s happened much later (in certain other eras), e.g. Shukla Yajur Veda Shatapatha Brahmana (Ekapaat Kanda 1/2/3), Nakshatra Sukta belonging to the Atharva Veda (Shaunaka Samhita 19/7/2), Maitrayaniya Aranyaka (6/14), and Taittiriya Brahmana (1/5/2).

For a wonderfully detailed exposition on the topic, see https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/dakshinayana-en and https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/uttarayana-en .

1986cd6c9d.d:
The Phalguna Paurnami festival is a grand five-day celebration held annually at the Swami Pushkarini. Each day of the festival features a different set of deities taken for a celestial ride on a beautifully decorated float in the temple tank.

1. On the first day, Bhagavan Rama, along with Sita and Lakshmana, are worshipped and taken for a ride on the float.
2. The second day is dedicated to Bhagavan Krishna and Rukmini, who are also offered puja and taken on the float for a pleasure ride.

For the last three days, from Trayodashi to Paurnami:
1. Sri Malayappa Swami, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, are taken out for a ride in the temple tank.
2. The third day includes three rounds of the float, increasing to five rounds on the next day.
3. On the final day, the utsava murtis (festival deities) are taken for a splendid ride on the float for seven rounds, attracting a large number of pilgrims. The beauty of the deities is further enhanced by the charm of the full moon, making this day particularly special and visually stunning.

19b2b342b2.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

This Nayanmar, a Vellala from Tirucchangamangai, grew disillusioned with worldly life and yearned for liberation. Initially swayed by Buddhist teachings, he eventually found his spiritual calling in Shaivism, convinced that intense devotion to Bhagavan Shiva was the true path to liberation. Despite maintaining the outward appearance of a Buddhist, his heart was devoted to Bhagavan Shiva.

In an unusual display of devotion, he would sit in an open Shiva temple, deeply meditating on the Lingam. One day, in a state of divine absorption, he unwittingly threw a stone at the Lingam. Realizing this act the next day, he interpreted it as divine will, understanding that Bhagavan Shiva accepts any offering made with sincere devotion. Henceforth, throwing a stone at the Lingam became his unique form of daily worship, a ritual he performed before eating.

On one occasion, just as he was about to eat, he remembered he had not performed his daily ritual. Driven by devotion, he rushed to the temple to throw a stone at the Lingam! Touched by his unorthodox yet profound devotion, Bhagavan Shiva appeared before him, blessed him, and ultimately took him to Kailasa, the abode of the divine.
19b2b342b2.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

19dbc2c1b0.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′01.05″.
19dbc2c1b0.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′01.05″, 0°40′56.20″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°06′35.70″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.17, elongation 16°01′11.68″ E). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°47′36.75″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.85, elongation 16°04′48.52″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1a29227417.d:
The Krishna-paksha Ekadashi of jyaiṣṭha month is known as yōginī-ēkādaśī.

The fruits of fasting on Ekādaśī are greatly extolled in the Padma Purana—

A person who bathes at Śaṃkhoddhāra and beholds the image of Viṣṇu does not acquire even a sixteenth of the merit earned by fasting on Ekādaśī. O noble king, even if one gives four lakhs of coins on the days of the Sun's transition between Zodiac signs, it does not equal even a sixteenth of the merit from an Ekādaśī fast! Indeed, fasting on Ekādaśī grants the same religious merit as bathing at Prabhāsa during a lunar or solar eclipse. One who drinks the sacred water at Kedāra is freed from rebirth, and likewise, fasting on Ekādaśī removes the cycle of rebirth.

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.
1a29227417.s:
𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌯𑌦𑍀𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌃।  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍁𑌭𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌿॥  
  
𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷 𑌶𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌮𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌦𑌥𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍇 𑌕𑍇𑌶𑌵 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵।  
𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚 𑌵𑍈 𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑍋 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌤𑌃॥  
--𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇  
  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌸𑍌𑌤𑌿𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃---  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇।  
𑌸 𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈𑌕𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋 𑌵𑌯𑌃॥௧௪॥  
  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌗𑌦𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௩௫॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌨𑍃𑌪𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮॥௩௬॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑍇 𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌃॥௩௭॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑍂𑌨𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌕𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌚𑍋𑌦𑌕𑌂 𑌪𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௩௮॥  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥 𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍀।  
𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍃𑌥𑌿𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௩௯॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍋 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌤𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌃॥௪௦॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑍂𑌨𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌗𑍋𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌗𑍇॥௪௧॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌯𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌃॥௪௨॥  
𑌵𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍁𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍋 𑌯𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌾𑌃॥௪௩॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌰𑍈𑌰𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌭𑌮𑍍॥௪௪॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌸𑌮𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௧௮॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌶𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌉𑌮𑌾𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿-𑌮𑍁𑌰𑌵𑌧𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌂𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃॥௪௦॥

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.

𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌣𑌮𑍍।

1a6b681858.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in mūlā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°18′37.71″.
1a6b681858.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°18′37.71″, 0°18′29.88″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°00′03.54″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.28, elongation 26°56′19.18″ E). śukraḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°18′41.25″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 26°57′03.52″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1a78224d62.d: When the Ekadashi tithi is incident at sunrise on two consecutive days, the second day, where there is association with Dvadashi tithi, is known as unmīlanī is one of the eight mahādvādaśīs. The day on which Ekādaśī continues through day and night and extends for a ghaṭikā into the next day is known as Unmīlanī, and it is especially beloved by Bhagavan Viṣṇu. The combined sanctity of all holy and sacred places in the three worlds pales in comparison to even a fraction of the merit of Unmīlanī, as do sacrifices and austerities. There has never been, nor will there ever be, anything like Unmīlanī! The moment one worships Bhagavan Viṣṇu on the Unmīlanī day, all their accumulated (heaps of) sins fall (away) instantly. O king, Bhagavan Viṣṇu should be worshipped with great effort, using the name of the month in which the Unmīlanī day occurs.
1a78224d62.s:

𑌉𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍀𑌲𑌨𑍀 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌾 𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑍇𑌣 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌾।

1a8e1b6bb9.d:
The celestial wedding of Bhagavan Srinivasa and Devi Padmavati is a grand festival held annually in the month of Vaishakha. The beautifully adorned Parinayotsavam Mandapam, set amidst the Narayanagiri gardens, serves as the enchanting venue for this three-day event, celebrated under the moonlit sky. The festivities unfold on the auspicious days of Navami, Dashami, and Ekadashi in the month of Vaishakha, featuring Sri Malayappaswami, Shri Venkateshwara's festival deity. Each day, he makes a grand entrance on different Vahanas: the Gaja (elephant), Ashva (horse), and Garuda (eagle), while Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi grace the event on separate palanquins.

Following the wedding rituals at the Parinayotsava Mandapam, a traditional 'Koluvu' gathering takes place, filled with the recitation of Vedic hymns and devotional songs. Bhagavan, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, then majestically returns to the temple.

Each day's festivities are marked by unique traditional rituals. On the first day, the arrival of Bhagavan Malayappa Swami on the celestial Gaja Vahanam, along with his consorts on their palanquins, is a sight to behold. The traditional wedding ceremony is conducted, where Bhagavan is seated in the ornately decorated Parinaya Mandapam, with his consorts positioned opposite him.

The ceremony includes several traditional rituals such as Edurukolu (mutual reception), Pula Bantata (game of flower balls), and Vastra Dharanam (offering of new clothes). These customs are observed over all three days. The grand finale of the divine marriage is marked by a spectacular display of fireworks, adding to the ceremony's splendor. The event concludes with a procession where Bhagavan Malayappa Swami, along with Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi, return to the main temple.

1ae6cd2af9.d: When a tripādanakṣatra is conjoined with a bhadrā tithi i.e. dvitīyā, saptamī or dvādaśī, and this falls on a Tuesday, Sunday or Saturday, it is known as a tripuṣkara-yōgaḥ. The dvipuṣkara occurs when the bhadrā tithis coincide with the same days as above, but with the dvipāda nakṣatras, which are mr̥gaśīrṣa, chitrā and dhaniṣṭhā. Like the tripuṣkara which gives a three-fold multiplier for śubha and aśubha, the dvipuṣkara has a two-fold effect.

1b47927547.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′44.86″.
1b47927547.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′44.86″, 0°57′40.55″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′14.56″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′19.46″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°56′59.42″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′24.65″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1b78277018.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Nagan, a skilled king of hunters from Uduppur in Pottapi Nadu, was a devout follower of Bhagavan Subramanya. He and his wife, Tattai, were blessed with a child named Tinnanar, who was believed to be the reincarnation of Arjuna. Tinnanar, raised as a hunter, excelled in archery and succeeded his father as the king at a young age. Despite his occupation, he practiced non-violence towards young ones, females, diseased animals, etc. and spiritually, he had already eliminated inner vices like lust, anger, greed, vanity, jealousy, etc.

One day, Tinnanar chased a pig that had escaped its net, leading to an intense pursuit that ended with Tinnanar killing the pig. Exhausted and thirsty, he and his companions sought water and rest. Tinnanar experienced a profound spiritual transformation as he climbed a nearby hill, losing his body consciousness and feeling an overwhelming love for Bhagavan Shiva. On the hill, he found a temple dedicated to Bhagavan Shiva and was moved to tears, feeling a deep connection with the deity.

Tinnanar's devotion led him to bring food to the temple daily, offering the best pieces of meat after tasting them himself. His actions disturbed his friends and family, who thought he had gone mad. One day, the temple's priest, Shivagochariar, was horrified to find the temple desecrated by Tinnanar's unconventional worship, which included water from his mouth for 'Abhishekam', and decoration of the Lingam with flowers worn on his head!

Despite Shivagochariar's efforts to purify the temple and conduct traditional worship, Tinnanar continued his practices, standing guard at the temple entrance after each of his rituals.

Shivagochariar prayed for intervention, and Bhagavan Shiva appeared in his dream and instructed him to witness Tinnanar's actions. On the sixth day, while at his usual quest to gather food for Bhagavan Shiva, Tinnanar encountered ominous signs. In his selfless devotion, Tinnanar was more concerned for the deity than for himself and these signs sparked a fear that something untoward had befallen Bhagavan!  Upon reaching the temple, he was devastated to find blood flowing from the deity's right eye. In his grief, he dropped all the worship items and tried to treat the deity's eye with herbs, but the bleeding persisted. Driven by a thought of equivalent sacrifice --- ‘flesh for flesh’ --- he removed his own right eye with an arrow and placed it on the deity, and the bleeding miraculously stopped. Overwhelmed with joy and dancing in ecstasy, he now noticed the deity's left eye bleeding. He was clear on how to stop this bleeding --- but how would he place the second eye having lost his vision? He planted his foot over the deity's left eye on the Lingam to guide himself! Just as he was about to extract his left eye, Bhagavan Shiva intervened, grasping his hand and affectionately addressing him as Kannappa (thrice), thus transforming Tinnanar into Kannappar. Bhagavan held him close, restoring his vision and granting him a divine status. Shivagochariar, the temple priest, witnessed this act of supreme devotion and understood its true nature.

The story also carries a deeper, symbolic meaning. Tinnanar's journey represents the spiritual conquest over inner evils, including ego (symbolized by the wild pig). Accompanied by representations of good and evil (Nanan and Kadan), Tinnanar's pursuit of the pig signifies the battle with one's own vices and the embrace of positive samskaras (impressions). The culmination of his journey, where he chooses to worship Bhagavan alone, symbolizes the ultimate renunciation of even good tendencies for pure, unadulterated devotion. Tinnanar's willingness to sacrifice his own eyes for the deity epitomizes complete self-surrender, the pinnacle of devotion that leads to divine revelation and realization.

1b9e2461cf.d:
Dakṣiṇāyana-puṇyakālaḥ. For dakṣiṇāyana, the 30 ghatikas preceding the saṅkramaṇa form a puṇyakāla; in general, the ghatikas closer to the puṇyakāla are even more sacred.

While the nirayana puṇyakāla-s are well known, marked by the transit of the Sun into various rāśī-s (which confer the name to the corresponding saura month), there are also ayana-s and sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s, which mark the position of the Sun above the Northern or Southern parts of the Earth. These determine the r̥tu-s, and also the very famous uttarāyaṇa and dakṣināyana (movement of the Sun towards North or South, respectively). While these two types of puṇyakāla-s (sāyana and nirayana) coincided millennia ago, there has been a gradual precession of the equinoxes, owing to the nature of the Earth's rotation, causing the sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s to happen about 24 days before the nirayana saṅkramaṇa-s. In that era, uttarāyaṇa coincided with makara-saṅkramaṇa and dakṣināyana coincided with karkaṭaka-saṅkramaṇa, and the mēsa and tulā saṅkramaṇa-s corresponded to the equinoxes, when the Sun rises direct East (and sets direct West).

Many Dharma Shastra texts recognise the separate puṇyakāla-s for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. The vachanam of Jaabaali Maharshi is mentioned above, where he says that the puṇyakāla-s are identical (in their reckoning) for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. In Kala Madhava, which is considered as the source text of the kala vicharas of the Dikshitiya, it is said in the 5th prakarana that,  meṣādi-saṅkrāntayo yasmin dine bhavanti tasmād dināt pūrvebhyaḥ ekādaśabhyo dinebhyaḥ prācīne dine, noting that Sayana Sankramanas occurred ~11 days before the day when the Mesha Sankramanas etc occur. Further references are seen in Dharma Sindhu first pariccheda, Jayasimha Kalpadruma sankranti nirnaya and Nirnaya Sindhu first pariccheda. There are also ample references in Vedas, illustrating how Ayana-s happened much later (in certain other eras), e.g. Shukla Yajur Veda Shatapatha Brahmana (Ekapaat Kanda 1/2/3), Nakshatra Sukta belonging to the Atharva Veda (Shaunaka Samhita 19/7/2), Maitrayaniya Aranyaka (6/14), and Taittiriya Brahmana (1/5/2).

For a wonderfully detailed exposition on the topic, see https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/dakshinayana-en and https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/uttarayana-en .

1ba685ccc1.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′23.62″.
1ba685ccc1.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′23.62″, 0°37′06.06″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.19″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′37.10″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′06.81″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.51″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1badf8ff40.d: Anadhyayana on account of aṣṭamī. Several tithis in a month are nitya-anadhyayana days, including prathamā, aṣṭamī, chaturdaśī, amāvāsyā and pūrṇimā. Manu has said that performing adhyayana on these days destroys the Guru (Amavasya), Shishya (Chaturdashi) and the vīrya of the brahma (vēda) itself (Ashtami/Purnima). Similarly, Jabali Rishi has said that Adhyayana on prathama hurts the buddhi while adhyayana on chaturdaśī hurts the brahma (vēda) itself!

1bc4d0c956.d: Beginning of śuchi-māsaḥ, marked by the transit of Sun into the 4th division of the tropical zodiac. Importantly, this also marks the beginning of dakṣiṇāyanam, and the end of uttarāyaṇam. This also marks the summer solstice. While nirayana saṅkrānti's are widely observed, tropical saṅkrānti's are also equally sacred, and have similar puṇyakālas associated with them.

1c6028a099.d: Budhaḥ sets into combustion (astamayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2025-Nov-16 05:34. At this moment budhaḥ is at anūrādhā-2 vr̥śchikaḥ (latitude 0°55′28.29″ S, moving vakra (retrograde)), magnitude +2.52, elongation 9°54′45.06″ E of the Sun. 1cc919ec9a.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°27′37.18″.
1cc919ec9a.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°27′37.18″, 0°27′26.46″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°36′42.55″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.17, elongation 22°36′42.22″ W). śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°09′05.37″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.93, elongation 22°33′56.55″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1e2b3092fc.b: Observed on Kr̥ṣṇa-Aṣṭamī tithi of Jyaiṣṭhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
1e2b3092fc.d:
The Wari (pilgrimage) is a centuries-old tradition in Maharashtra, India, involving a ceremonial procession of devotees (Warkaris) accompanying the Padukas (symbolic footprints) of saints to the Vithoba temple in Pandharpur. The two most prominent processions originate from the towns of Dehu and Alandi.

The procession of Sant Dnyaneshwar, affectionately known as Mauli (māūlī), begins one day later than the Dehu Yatra, from Āl̤andī on Jyeshtha Vadya Ashtami. This route is slightly shorter than the Dehu route but is equally arduous and spiritually significant. It often meets the Tukaram Pālkhī at specific junctures or converges near Pune before proceeding separately. Departing from the Samadhi Mandir, the Pālkhī moves to Pune, staying at the Pālkhī Vithoba Mandir in Bhavani Peth. The most visually dramatic leg of the journey follows as the devotees pull the heavy chariot up the steep Dive Ghat to reach Sāswaḍ, where the Pālkhī stays for two days. The route traverses the historic town of Jejuri—sacred to Lord Khandoba—and the village of Vālhe. Upon entering the Satara district, the procession halts at Loṇanda, famous for its unique sheep Ringan, and then Taraḍgaon. The journey continues through the princely town of Phalṭaṇ and onto Baraḍ. As it enters Solapur district, the halts include Nātepute, Māl̤shiras, and Vel̤āpūr, which hosts a spectacular Ringan. After a stop at Bhaṇḍīshegaon, the Mauli Pālkhī also arrives at Wākhari on Ashadhi Shuddha Dashami.

1e2cf1a947.d: Bhādrapada-māsaḥ begins today --- As stated in the Mahābhārata, a person who observes the month with the discipline of eating only once a day (ekāhāra) attains immense and incomparable wealth, beginning with riches and prosperity. 1e9715601a.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′42.03″.
1e9715601a.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′42.03″, 0°51′19.08″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′50.47″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°43′04.65″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′32.50″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′41.92″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
